title: Fringe Show 20: Bellringers ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ @Edinburgh Festival Fringe #edfr...
transcript: I love how subjective art can be because maybe one of the most divisive shows at the fringe between me and my friends was Bell Ringers. Bell Ringers is a new two hander play by Daisy Hall that takes place in a dystopian future in a village where the people have to ring the bells in order to, what they believe, clear these apocalyptic storms that keep happening in the village. However, as these storms get, keep getting worse and worse, because we're getting closer and closer to the apocalypse, uh, the likelihood that they die ringing these bells increases, because what's been happening is people have been getting struck by lightning while ringing the bells. It is the belief of many people in this village, like to a religious extent, that if they don't ring the bells, the storms won't clear. So the entire play is that them waiting for this storm to arrive and deciding whether or not they're gonna ring these bells. It is essentially a waiting for Godot or even a Rosenkrantz and Guildenstern are dead, but like, with apocalyptic stakes. And I loved it. I was engrossed from the second. Also, it helped that, like, there was these really cool storm sound effects, but at the same time there was a storm outside of, like, the cylindrical tent thing that we were in, so the wind was actually like blowing the tent and you could see the wind blowing as the storm was happening on Stage, so it almost felt like an immersive experience. There are so many things I loved about this play. One was the world building. Like, the fact that it was very much an apocalyptic, futuristic tale that felt like it was set in the past. There's a. There's a name for that, and I cannot think of it. If you know it, drop in the comments. And so it gives the entire play this kind of timeless but, like, fantastical feel to it. And then the questions that this play raises, like, what would you do? And what would you sacrifice to save, uh, an entire community? What would you do to save your friends? Um, you know what, what do you prioritize more, saving the group or saving your friend? This is essentially just a, like, very, uh, theatrical trolley problem set in an apocalyptic future. And then there's the aspect of religion in this play, because one of the characters is an atheist, and one believes what he's been taught by the church. And both of them are taught by the church that the. What they need to do is ring these bells to clear the storm. So there's so many questions of, like, religious belief, and do you believe it even when it could cost you your own life? And there's so many of those fascinating existential questions in this play. Um, plus the relationship between these two men on stage, um, and their friendship and the Impending tension of the storm that you hear go coming closer and closer. And the build up of all of those things together kept me engaged the entire time. And if that's enough to keep you engaged, then this is probably a play that you would rather like. If the thought of sitting through something like a waiting for Godot with, you know, a storm sounds miserable, this is definitely not the play for you. It's very much in that same vein. I did personally find this easier to understand that a lot of Samuel Beckett's work, um, which I think sometimes can be a little too absurdist for my consciousness, um, this. This, to me, just made sense the entire time. But if you struggle with that kind of theater, again, this is probably not for you. I personally really enjoyed it and immediately bought it afterwards. And I cannot wait to read it, to kind of dive into more of the text and more of what Daisy Hall's presenting in the show. And at the end of the day, I love plays that get a little existential, and this was absolutely that.
